No, the Great Wall of China is not visible from space

Astronauts have said it for decades and the optics confirm it. At 400 kilometers up, the Great Wall is roughly ten times too narrow for the human eye to resolve, and its color barely stands out from the ground around it.

The Great Wall of China at Jinshanling, Severin Stalder (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0)

The gist. The claim that the Great Wall of China is visible from space, or even from the Moon, with the naked eye is false. At low Earth orbit the wall is about ten times narrower than the human eye can resolve, and its stone blends into the surrounding terrain. Every astronaut who has looked for it agrees.

Ask a classroom which human structure can be seen from space and most hands go up for the same answer, the Great Wall of China. It is one of the stickiest facts that is not actually a fact, repeated in textbooks, trivia nights and even some museum placards. The physics of the human eye settles it in a couple of lines of arithmetic.

The earliest known version predates spaceflight by two centuries. English antiquarian William Stukeley speculated in a 1754 letter that a wall so massive "might likely be seen from the moon." The idea resurfaced in 1938 in Richard Halliburton's bestselling Second Book of Marvels , which stated flatly that "astronomers say" the wall was the only human made object visible from the Moon, without naming a single astronomer. Artificial structures visible from space

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Human-made things that can be seen from space

Artificial structures visible from space without magnification include highways, dams, and cities. [ 1 ] [ 2 ]

Whether an object is visible depends significantly on the height above sea level from where it is observed. The Kármán line , at 100 kilometres (62   mi) , is accepted by the World Air Sports Federation , an international standard-setting and record-keeping body for aeronautics and astronautics , as the boundary between the Earth's atmosphere and outer space . [ 3 ] However, astronauts typically orbit the Earth at several hundreds of kilometres; [ 4 ] the ISS , for example, orbits at about 420   km (260   mi) above the Earth, [ 5 ] and the Moon orbits at about 380,000   km (240,000   mi) away. [ 4 ]

From US Space Shuttles , which typically orbited at around 135   mi (217   km) , cities were easily distinguishable from surrounding countryside. [ 1 ] Using binoculars, astronauts could even see roads, dams, harbors, even large vehicles such as ships and planes. [ 2 ] [ 6 ] At night, cities are also easily visible from the higher orbit of the ISS.

Metropolitan areas are clearly visible at night, particularly in industrialized countries, due to a multitude of street lights and other light sources in urban areas (see light pollution ).

In October 2003, after the first Chinese astronaut Yang Liwie returned from his first journey into Space, a popular belief was apparently called into question when he stated that he had not been able to see the Great Wall of China. Liwie's observation contradicted the information previously presented in several books, board games and various television contests, to quote a few examples. After Liwie's declarations, the Chinese government asked for his statement to be removed from various reports.
